title: MA8-12007
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Gabon, is basing his claim for refugee protection on section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant was hired in 1995 in the city of XXXX, Gabon, where the main industry is mining. His problems began around 2007, following the founding of a group of protesters whose goal was to denounce the violation of ecological rules and the cancellation of workers' medical coverage at the company's hospital.

In 2008, he XXXX XXXX to raise awareness in the neighbouring villages. During a protest on XXXX, 2008, soldiers arrested him and took him to the police station, where he was beaten with police batons. Only a few hours later, he was forced into a military vehicle and taken to the military base in XXXX.

During the trip, one of the high-ranking officers who was watching him asked him what ethnic group he belonged to. When the claimant told him that he was of the XXXX ethnic group, this man promised to release him, since he was of the same ethnicity. Thus, the claimant was released with this man's help and hitchhiked home. When he arrived, he asked his wife to contact a friend in Canada and have him send a letter of invitation as a visitor to Canada.

On XXXX, 2008, he went to Cameroon to file his application at the Canadian High Commission. He received his visa eight days later. He returned to Gabon in secret. On XXXX, 2008, he travelled to XXXX, and then arrived in Montréal on XXXX, 2008. He claimed Canada's protection on XXXX, 2008.

Having heard the claimant's testimony and analyzed all of the evidence on file, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection," for the reasons that follow.

To begin, the claimant states in his narrative that he founded a group of protesters for the purpose of reaching the majority of people living in the villages in order to obtain free medical care and benefits, and also to denounce the violation of ecological rules.

When he was asked whether the association he had founded had a name, he answered that it did not. He was also asked whether he had a copy of the letter he had sent to the authorities a few days before he participated in this protest on XXXX, XXXX, 2008. He answered that he did not have a copy of this letter because it had been written in the name of XXXX XXXX and he had not kept a copy. In light of these responses, the panel is of the opinion that his claims about XXXX XXXX are wholly insufficient, and the panel strongly doubts that he was a member of this pressure group.

Another element that casts doubt on his responsibilities as XXXX XXXX was noted in his testimony regarding the other five members of this association. The panel asked him whether he knew what had happened to the other five people who, like him, had participated in the protest on XXXX, XXXX, 2008. He answered that he had gotten news of them when he called the union after arriving in Canada. He testified that, according to the union, three of these people were considered disappeared, as they had not responded to the call that was sent out to them. He stated that the other two people had been able to go back to work for the company.

The panel asked him why the other two people, who had been responsible, as XXXX, for the protest on XXXX, 2008, had been able to return to work, whereas he had received death threats. The claimant responded that he thought he had been threatened because he was a XXXX in the XXXX XXXX mining company. He was also asked why he XXXX XXXX -person committee to protest against the activities of the company he was working for, at the same time as the local representative of the XXXX XXXX pour XXXX et le XXXX [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX] had formed a pressure group rallying all the inhabitants of the mining city of XXXX to protest the XXXX mining company's violation of ecological rules. A document dated XXXX, 2008,1 (an article entitled "Gabon : Moanda pointe du doigt la pollution de la COMILOG" [Gabon: Moanda denounces COMILOG pollution]) clearly states the following: [Translation] [L]ed by the local representative of the Union gabonaise pour la démocratie et le développement [Gabonese Union for Democracy and Development], inhabitants of the mining city of Moanda in the province of Haut-Ogooué protested vehemently against the Comilog mining company's violation of ecological rules, at a recent meeting of the company's governing board. In particular, protesters demanded the reinstatement of free health care in the company's medical facilities. And further: [I]nhabitants of the commune of Moanda pointed a finger at the Ogoouée mining company, Comilog, at the most recent meeting of its governing board, denouncing Comilog's violation of ecological rules and the cancellation of its medical coverage for workers.2 Led by Valentin Leyama, the representative of the Union gabonaise pour la démocratie et le développement, inhabitants called on officials to rehabilitate the areas polluted by the company's dumping of its industrial waste.

The claimant was therefore asked why he XXXX XXXX for the same purpose as the committee under this organization founded by the local representative, who moreover lived in the same area as the claimant; he was further asked what he was expecting, as an employee heading a small group could not have as great an impact as the XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX. The claimant responded that the representative was not from the same province as him, that he was from XXXX, XXXX. The panel does not accept the claimant's testimony, as this representative was inciting the inhabitants of XXXX to protest against XXXX. It is clear that the claimant was not aware of this well-known protest led by the local representative.

In addition, when he was asked whether he had left or quit his job, the claimant stated that he had never contacted his employer at work and that, according to the information he had received from the union, he had lost his job because the company took a negative view of him.

Furthermore, after obtaining a letter of invitation from a Canadian he had allegedly met in XXXX while he was working at the mine, the claimant went to XXXX to obtain his Canadian visa. He therefore went to XXXX twice to obtain his Canadian visa, and returned to XXXX without even trying to settle in XXXX. When the panel asked him why he had not considered staying in XXXX, he answered that he had not intended to claim asylum there, and then added that he would not have been safe in XXXX and that that was why he had returned to XXXX, a country where he claims he was being persecuted. The panel believes that the claimant had no fear of returning to his country, because if he had truly feared for his life, he would never have voluntarily returned to XXXX, as he did on two occasions.

In addition, the claimant's response regarding why he had not claimed refugee protection upon his arrival in Canada on XXXX, 2008, was not satisfactory in the panel's opinion. The claimant had previously testified that he would be a dead man if he returned to his country. When asked to explain his conduct, he stated that he had planned to stay here and work and that he had not realized that there were procedures to follow.

Once again, the panel does not believe that the claimant has a fear of returning. His entire testimony leads the panel to believe that he came here to have access to better economic opportunities because, as noted above, if he feared for his life, he would have claimed protection immediately, the moment he arrived in Canada. The fact that he returned to XXXX twice, without finding a way to take refuge, casts doubt on his fear of returning to his country. Moreover, the panel notes in this regard that the case law has consistently held that a refugee protection claimant's voluntary return to their country of nationality is inconsistent with a well-founded fear of persecution.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant has not discharged his burden of proof. Consequently, the claim for refugee protection filed by XXXX XXXX is rejected. Anna-Maria Silvestri Me Anna-Maria Silvestri November 29, 2010 Date IRB translation Original language: French REFUGEE PROTECTION DIVISION / VICTIM OF CRIMINALITY / VISA / VISITOR / FAILURE TO SEEK PROTECTION IN OTHER COUNTRIES / REAVAILMENT / MALE / NEGATIVE / GABON 1 Exhibit P-5, newspaper articles (in a bundle) see "Gabon : Moanda pointe du doigt la pollution de la COMILOG" [Gabon: Moanda denounces COMILOG pollution]. 2 Ibid., p. 1. --------------- --------------- --------------- --------------- RPD File No. / No de dossier de la SPR : MA8-12007 5
